column2: Then the mighty-bowed Parthas quickly rushed in chariots at the king who had been approached by Satyaki, wishing to slay their maternal uncle.
Then a tumultuous crush took place with blood for water, of the brave fighting, like lions roaring.
There was a mutual clash among them, O great king, like lions in battle crying out, desirous of prey.
The earth was strewn with floods of their thousands of arrows, and the sky suddenly became full of arrows.
A darkness of arrows was made in many ways there on every side, a shade as of cloud arose from the arrows loosed by the great souls.
There, O king, the quarters shone with arrows loosed as if serpents freed from their skins, with golden feathers, shining.
Shalya, slayer of foes, did a supreme marvel there, in that alone, the brave one, he fought many in the battle.
The earth was strewn with dreadful arrows falling, loosed from the arms of the king of the Madras, heron-feathered.
There we saw Shalya's chariot ranging in the great battle as of old Shakra's in the destruction of the asuras.
Tormented, all your men, arrogant in battle, ran forward, and in a moment, by their numbers, they overwhelmed the Parthas.
Slain by the Kurus, the Pandavas did not stand, though held back by Bhima, in the sight of Krishna and Partha.
Then Dhananjaya, enraged, covered Kripa with his followers and Kritavarman with a flood of arrows.
Sahadeva held Shakuni back with his army; Nakula, standing at the side, looked at the king of the Madras.
The sons of Draupadi mostly held back the kings, and Shikhandin the Panchala held back Drona's son.
Bhimasena, mace in hand, held back the king (Duryodhana), and Kunti's son Yudhishthira held back Shalya with his army.
Then a battle took place, locked together here and there, of yours and the enemy's, never retreating from battles.
We saw there Shalya's very great deed in the battle: that alone he fought all the armies of the Pandavas.
Having tormented the king (Yudhishthira) with arrows like venomous serpents, he rushed on and covered Bhima with showers of arrows.
Seeing his dexterity and skill with weapons, the divisions of yours and the enemy honoured it.
Tormented by Shalya, the Pandavas, much wounded, fled from the battle while Yudhishthira cried out.

While the divisions were being slain by the king of the Madras, the Pandava, the king of dharma Yudhishthira, fell under the power of indignation; then taking up manliness, he tormented the king of the Madras.
Victory or death—so resolved, the great chariot-warrior summoned all his brothers and Krishna Madhava and said:

Bhishma, Drona and Karna, and the other lords of the earth who were valiant for the Kauravas' sake, have gone to their end in the battle.
mahabharata:9:15.17	You have all done manly deeds according to your share and zeal; one share remains for me: this great chariot-warrior Shalya.
mahabharata:9:15.18	Today I hope to conquer the lord of the Madras in battle; what is in my mind regarding this, I tell you all.
mahabharata:9:15.19	These two heroes, the sons of Madri, my wheel-guards, unconquerable even by Vasava in battle, esteemed heroes,
mahabharata:9:15.20	well may they, putting kshatriya duty first, fight their maternal uncle for my sake, worthy of honour and true to their pledge.
mahabharata:9:15.21	Either Shalya will slay me in the battle or I him; good luck to you. Hear this true word, heroes of the world:
mahabharata:9:15.22	today I shall fight my uncle by kshatriya duty, O lords of the earth, having myself resolved, for victory or the other.
mahabharata:9:15.23	Let my chariot-yokers quickly equip me in the battle with superior weapons and all equipment according to rule.
mahabharata:9:15.24	Let Shaineya be my right wheel, Dhrishtadyumna the left, and Partha Dhananjaya my rear-guard today.
mahabharata:9:15.25	Let Bhima, best of weapon-bearers, go before me today; so I shall be superior to Shalya in the great battle.
Thus addressed, all the kings, wishing his good, did so; and joy of the armies arose again then, O king,
of the Panchalas, Somakas and especially the Matsyas, fulfilling the king of dharma's pledge in the battle.
Then the Panchalas sounded conches, kettledrums and hundreds of drums and uttered lion-roars.
Those mighty ones rushed in fury at the king of the Madras with a great sound born of joy, the bulls of the Kurus.
With the clamour of elephant-bells, the sound of conches and the great noise of instruments, they made the earth resound.
Your son and the valiant king of the Madras received them, as two mountains, east and west, receive many great clouds.
Shalya, proud of war, rained a shower of arrows on the king of dharma, tamer of foes, as Maghavan rains.
Likewise the Kuru king, taking a fair bow, showing the many teachings of Drona, the high-minded,
rained showers of arrows, wondrous, swift and well; nobody saw any opening in him as he ranged in the battle.
Those two hewed each other with arrows of many kinds, like tigers desirous of prey, valiant in battle.
Bhima met your son, skilled in war; the Panchala, Satyaki and the two sons of Madri confronted on every side the heroes led by Shakuni.
Then a tumultuous battle took place again of yours and the enemy's, eager for victory, O king, through your ill counsel.
Duryodhana, with a straight-jointed arrow, aimed in battle, cut Bhima's gold-adorned banner.
With a great net of little bells, the fair-looking lion of Bhimasena's banner fell roaring.
And the lord of men again cut his variegated bow, like an elephant-king's trunk, with a sharp-edged razor-arrow.
With his bow cut, the glorious one, by valour pierced your son in the chest with a chariot-dart, and he sank on the chariot seat.
While he was in stupor, Vrikodara again struck off the charioteer's head from his body with a razor-arrow.
With his charioteer slain, his horses took the chariot and fled in all directions, O king, and a cry of "Alas" arose then.
Drona's son, the great chariot-warrior, ran to save him, as did Kripa and Kritavarman, wishing to protect your son.
While that army was in disorder and his followers terrified, the Gandiva-bowman, stretching his bow, struck them with arrows.
Yudhishthira, indignant, rushed at the lord of the Madras, himself urging his ivory-white horses swift as mind.
There we saw a marvel in Kunti's son Yudhishthira: though he had been gentle and self-controlled before, he then became terrible.
With wide eyes, trembling with anger, the son of Kunti cut warriors with sharp arrows by hundreds of thousands.
Whichever army that eldest Pandava advanced on, he felled it with arrows, O king, as the best thunderbolts fell mountains.
Felling many chariot-warriors with their horses, charioteers, banners and chariots, he played alone, strong, like the wind with clouds.
He crushed horses with riders and foot-soldiers by thousands in the battle, enraged, like Rudra animals.
Having emptied the battlefield with showers of arrows on every side, he rushed at the king of the Madras and said, "Stand, Shalya!"
Seeing that deed of his of terrible work in the battle, all your men were terrified; but Shalya advanced against him.
Then those two, much enraged, sounded their conches born of water, challenged one another and came together, rebuking.
Shalya covered Yudhishthira with a shower of arrows, and the son of Kunti covered the king of the Madras with showers of arrows.
The two heroes, the king of the Madras and Yudhishthira, were seen then, O king, in the battle with heron-feathered arrows, blood streaming.
They shone like flowering silk-cotton and kimshuka trees in a forest, those two great souls blazing, arrogant in the battle of lives.
Seeing it, all the armies could not decide the victory of either: "Partha will enjoy the earth today having slain the lord of the Madras,"
or "Shalya having slain the Pandava will give the earth to Duryodhana"—there was no such certainty among the warriors there, O Bharata.
Everything circled to the right for the fighting king of dharma.
Then Shalya quickly loosed a hundred arrows at Yudhishthira and cut his bow with a sharp-pointed arrow.
Taking another bow, he pierced Shalya with three hundred arrows, and cut his bow with a razor-arrow.
Then he killed his four horses with straight-jointed arrows, and with two sharp-pointed ones the two heel-guards and charioteer.
Then with a bright yellow sharp broad-headed arrow he took off the banner as he stood in front; then Duryodhana's army, tamer of foes, broke.
Then Drona's son rushed at the lord of the Madras and, placing him thus on his own chariot, hurriedly fled.
Having gone a moment, with Yudhishthira roaring, the lord of the Madras halted and mounted another chariot,
duly prepared, white, resounding like a great cloud, with all machines and equipment, hair-raising to foes.
Then, immeasurable-souled, bull among kshatriyas, he rained a shower of arrows on the kshatriyas like a rain-bearing cloud.
Piercing Satyaki with ten, Bhimasena with three arrows, and Sahadeva with three, he tormented Yudhishthira.
He, best of chariot-warriors, slew those and other mighty archers with horses, chariots and elephants: elephants, elephant-riders, horses, horse-men, and chariots with chariot-warriors.
He cut arms with their weapons and banners and made the earth strewn with warriors as an altar with kusha grass.
As he slew enemy armies like Death the ender, the Pandavas, Panchalas and Somakas, much enraged, surrounded him.
Bhimasena, Shini's grandson and the two noble sons of Madri together filled the king (Shalya) of mighty strength, challenging one another.
Then the brave warriors, meeting in the battle the lord of the Madras, best of warriors, surrounded him and struck him with fierce-speed feathered arrows.
Guarded by Bhimasena, the king, the sons of Madri and Madhava, the son of Dharma struck the lord of the Madras in the chest with fierce-speed feathered arrows.
Drawn to the ear and loosed, with arrows washed in oil, the two great chariot-warriors, the lord of the Madras and Yudhishthira, covered each other.
Then those two great chariot-warriors, swiftly in the battle, looking for each other's opening, pierced each other hard with arrows, the best of kings, mighty and unassailable by foes.
A great sound of their bowstring and palms arose, like the sound of Mahendra's thunderbolt, as the two great souls, the Madra and the Pandava hero, rained arrows on each other.
They ranged like tiger cubs in great forests, eager for prey, like two tusked noble elephants, and hewed each other, proud from the fight.
Then the great-souled lord of the Madras forcibly pierced Yudhishthira, of Bhima-like strength, in the heart with an arrow of exceeding speed bright as sun and fire.
Deeply pierced, Yudhishthira, the great soul, bull of the Kurus, struck the lord of the Madras with a well-aimed arrow and rejoiced.
Then in a moment, the lord of the earth regained consciousness, his eyes red with rage, and swiftly struck Partha with a hundred, equal to the thousand-eyed one in power.
Then in haste the great-souled son of Dharma, enraged, piercing Shalya's golden armour and chest with nine arrows, struck him with six more.
Then the delighted lord of the Madras, drawing his bow, loosed arrows, and with two razor-arrows cut the bow of the king, the bull of the Kurus.
Then the great-souled king took another dreadful bow in the battle and pierced Shalya with sharp arrows on every side, as Mahendra Namuchi with sharp points.
Then Shalya with nine arrows each cut the strong armour of gold of Bhima and of King Yudhishthira and split the arms of the great soul.
Then with another razor-arrow, bright as the blazing sun, he struck off the king's bow, and Kripa killed his charioteer with six arrows; he fell facing him.
The lord of the Madras killed Yudhishthira's horses with four arrows, and having killed the horses, the great soul destroyed the king of dharma's followers.
With the king thus treated, the great soul Bhimasena quickly cut the lord of the Madras' bow with a swift arrow and pierced the lord of men hard with two.
With another he took the driver's head from his body amid his armour, and swiftly killed his four horses, Bhimasena greatly enraged.
Leader of all bowmen, he ranging alone, very swift in the battle, Bhima, and the son of Madri Sahadeva covered him with a hundred arrows.
Seeing Shalya bewildered by those arrows, Bhima cut his armour with arrows; and the lord of the Madras, whose armour was cut by Bhimasena, took a shield with a thousand stars.
Taking a sword and leaping from the chariot, the great soul rushed at Kunti's son; cutting Nakula's chariot-pole, he ran, of Bhima-like strength, at Yudhishthira.
As the king leapt up, coming like enraged Death, Dhrishtadyumna, the sons of Draupadi, Shikhandin and the grandson of Shini suddenly surrounded him.
Then great-souled Bhima cut his incomparable shield with ten arrows and cut his sword at the hilt with broad-headed arrows, roaring, delighted, amid your army.
Seeing that deed of Bhima, the foremost chariot-throngs of the Pandavas were glad and gave great cries, smiling greatly, and blew conches white as the moon.
By that fearful sound, the scorched, joyless army, overcome with sweat, drenched in blood, as if senseless and dejected—
that king of the Madras, suddenly scattered by the Pandava warriors led by Bhima, rushed with speed at Yudhishthira like a lion at its prey.
Seeing the lord of the Madras with his horses and charioteer slain, the king of dharma, blazing with anger, quickly rushed at that foe with force.
Quickly recalling Govinda's words, he resolved to destroy Shalya; standing on the chariot whose horses and charioteer were slain, the king of dharma desired a dart.
Hearing that deed of Shalya, the great soul, remembering the portion remaining of his share, self-controlled, he resolved on Shalya's slaying, as stated by Indra's younger brother (Krishna).
The king of dharma took a dart with a jewelled golden shaft, bright as gold, and suddenly opening his blazing eyes, looked at the lord of the Madras with an angry mind.
Looked at by the king, the pure-souled one with his sins removed, that the lord of the Madras was not reduced to ash seems to me a marvel, O king.
Then the great soul, the foremost of the Kurus, hurled with force that fair, fierce-shafted dart, blazing with jewels and coral, at the lord of the Madras.
All the Kurus gathered saw it falling suddenly, blazing, with great force, with sparks, like a great meteor at the end of an age.
The king of dharma, with effort, loosed that unfailing dart, like Night of Time with noose in hand, like Yama's fierce nurse, like Brahma's rod.
Honoured by the sons of Pandu with perfume, garlands, best seats, drink and food, blazing like the fire of destruction, a sorcery like the fierce Atharvangirasa,
made by Tvashtri for Ishana's sake, eater of the bodies of foes, able to slay by force beings in earth, sky, waters and lakes,
bearing bells, banners, jewels and diamonds, variegated with lapis lazuli, with a golden shaft, made by Tvashtri with effort and discipline, destroyer of Brahma's enemies, unfailing,
of speed raised by strength and effort, consecrated with dreadful mantras, he loosed it on its supreme course for the slaying of the lord of the Madras.
Roaring "You are slain!", with his arm outstretched, hand firm, as Rudra for the Ender, as if dancing in anger, the king of dharma
loosed that dart with all his might; and Shalya, not able to hold back its force, roared to receive it as fire receives well-poured ghee.
It split his bright, broad chest and his armour and entered the earth like water unobstructed, burning the king's wide fame.
With the blood streaming from his nose, eyes, ears and mouth and from the wound, his limbs were drenched in blood, like the great mountain Krauncha struck by Skanda.
With arms outstretched, fallen from his chariot to the earth, his armour cut by the delight of the Kurus, that great soul, like Mahendra's mount, like the peak of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt,
with arms outspread facing the king of dharma, the lord of the Madras fell to the ground like a raised banner of Indra.
With all his limbs pierced, drenched in blood, that best of men lay as if embraced by the earth in love.
As a lover falls on the breast of his dear beloved, having long enjoyed the earth, his dear beloved, the lord seemed to have fallen asleep, embracing her with all his limbs.
Slain by the righteous son of Dharma in righteous battle, he lay at peace like a well-offered fire quenched at a sacrifice.
Even though his heart was split by the dart and his weapon and banner struck, glory did not leave the lord of the Madras, though he lay at peace.
Then Yudhishthira took his bow, radiant as Indra's, and in the battle destroyed his foes, as the king of birds serpents, taking the lives of enemy bodies with sharp broad-headed arrows in a moment.
Then your soldiers, covered with floods of Partha's arrows, with eyes shut, tormented one another, with armour laid aside, weapons lost and lives gone from their bodies.
Then, when Shalya had fallen, the young younger brother of the king of the Madras, equal to his brother in every virtue, a chariot-warrior, advanced on the Pandava.
The best of men pierced him with many iron arrows in haste, wishing to avenge his slain brother, arrogant in battle.
The king of dharma pierced him with six swift arrows, as if in haste, cut his bow with two razor-arrows and also his banner.
Then with a blazing, firm, sharp broad-headed arrow he struck off his head as he stood in front.
That head with fair earrings was seen falling from the chariot, like a dweller in heaven, his merit exhausted, falling.
His body, its head severed, fell from the chariot, drenched in blood, and seeing it the army broke.
When the king of the Madras' younger brother, with his variegated armour, was slain, the Kurus fled, crying "Alas."
Seeing Shalya's younger brother slain, your men, giving up life, trembled from fear of the Pandavas, greatly shaken by dust.
As the Kauravas, terrified, broke thus, O best of the Bharatas, Shini's grandson Satyaki advanced, scattering arrows.
As that mighty archer came, irresistible and hard to approach, Hardikya swiftly and fearlessly received him, O king.
Those two great souls, unconquered Vrishnis, Hardikya and Satyaki, met like two lions in rut.
Covering each other with arrows of spotless lustre, they were like two suns with halos, bright as sun.
We saw in the sky the arrows of the two lions of the Vrishnis, driven by the strength of their bows, like swift locusts.
Hardikya, piercing Satyaki with ten and his horses with three arrows, cut his bow with a straight-jointed arrow.
Casting aside that cut best of bows, the bull of the Shinis swiftly took another, swifter weapon.
Taking that excellent bow, best of all bowmen, he pierced Hardikya in the chest with ten arrows.
Then, cutting his chariot-pole with well-aimed broad-headed arrows, he swiftly killed his horses and his two heel-guards.
With the king of the Madras slain and Kritavarman chariotless, all Duryodhana's force turned away again.
The enemy did not know, the army being covered with dust; the force, mostly slain, was turned away.
Then in a moment they saw the dust raised from the earth quenched by various streams of blood, O best of men.
Then Duryodhana, seeing his army broken from nearby, alone held back all the Parthas as they rushed with speed.
Seeing the Pandavas with their chariots, and Dhrishtadyumna the Parshata, and the invincible Anarta, he covered them with sharp arrows.
The enemy mortals did not face him, who seemed to have come as Death; then Hardikya, mounting another chariot, returned.
Then King Yudhishthira, the great chariot-warrior, in haste killed Kritavarman's horses with four feathered arrows and pierced Gautama with six sharp broad-headed arrows.
Then Ashvatthaman carried Hardikya, made horseless and chariotless by the king, away from Yudhishthira in his own chariot.
Then Sharadvata (Kripa) pierced Yudhishthira with eight, and pierced his horses with eight stone-pointed arrows.
Thus this remainder of the battle went on, O great king, through your ill counsel, with your sons, O Bharata.
When that best mighty archer was slain in the midst of the battle by the bull of the Kurus, the Parthas gathered, greatly delighted, and blew their conches, seeing Shalya slain.
They praised Yudhishthira in the battle, as the gods did Indra at the slaying of Vritra, and made sounds of instruments of many kinds, making the earth resound on every side.
Duryodhana, mounted on an elephant like a mountain, with a parasol held over him and fanned with fly-whisks, held back the Madras, saying "Do not go, do not go."
Held back again and again by Duryodhana, those heroes, wishing to kill Yudhishthira, entered the Pandava force.
Those brave ones, O great king, resolved in battle, making a great sound of bows, fought the Pandavas.
Hearing that Shalya was slain and the son of Dharma harassed, the great chariot-warriors of the Madrakas, intent on the king of the Madras' wish,
then Partha came, twanging Gandiva, the great chariot-warrior, filling all quarters with the roar of his chariot.
Then Arjuna, Bhima, the two sons of Madri, Satyaki the tiger among men, and the sons of Draupadi in full,
Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin, the Panchalas with the Somakas, wishing to protect Yudhishthira, surrounded him on every side.
Surrounded on all sides by the Pandavas, those bulls among men agitated that army like sea-monsters the sea.
Many cried out there, "Where is that King Yudhishthira? Not one of his brothers, those heroes, is seen."
The mighty Panchalas, and the great chariot-warrior Shikhandin, Dhrishtadyumna, Shaineya, and the sons of Draupadi in full—
As they spoke thus, the great chariot-warrior sons of Draupadi and Yuyudhana slew those heroes, followers of the king of the Madras.
Some were seen slain by the enemy in the battle with chariots crushed, and some with great banners cut.
Then the great chariot-warriors Kripa and Bhoja fell under sleep, accustomed to comfort and undeserving of pain; they lay on the ground, those two, O great king, wearied and grief-stricken.
By grieving one does not gain wealth, by grieving one does not find happiness, by grieving one does not gain fortune, by grieving one does not find the highest.
Pritha, it is said, again told him of the broad chest: 'Give safety to four; fight Phalguna as you wish.'
By his word I was bitten, not from anger or desire; in him, hunter, if there is a fault, it is a fault.
Let this be a very great pleasure to me, holder of discus and mace, glorious one, with a pleased mind, as long as you rejoice.
The king of dharma, Bhima, Savyasachin and the twins followed all that, looking to Dhritarashtra's wishes.
Mice multiplied, roads cracked, and mynas chirped "chee, chee, koochee" in the houses of the Vrishnis; and the noise did not stop by day or night.
Dhananjaya did not give up the divine bow Gandiva, nor, from greed for gems, the two great inexhaustible quivers, O great king.
And this I regret again and again, gods: that the feet of that immeasurably vigorous one are like my mother's.
